chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from some of our companions from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

Ahmad ibn al-Qasim wrote to him regarding a man who performed Umrah al-Mut'ah (Umrah followed by Hajj) but did not have what to offer as a sacrificial animal, so he fasted for three days. When he returned to his family, he was unable to fast the seven days [of the sacrifice], so he wanted to give food in charity. He asked: 'On how much should he give charity?' He wrote back: 'There is no alternative to fasting.'

His statement 'he was unable to fast' means he is unable to do so except with hardship, because if he were completely unable to fast under any circumstances, the Imam (peace be upon him) would not have said to him 'There is no alternative to fasting.'

key_terms.لَا بُدَّ مِنَ: There is no alternative to / It is obligatory

ai.seo_question: What is the compensation for a pilgrim who cannot afford a sacrificial animal during Umrah al-Mut'ah?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the compensation for a Mutamatti' pilgrim lacking a sacrificial animal, ruling that fasting is mandatory rather than optional fidya. The Imam’s specific phrasing indicates that fasting is required even if it entails hardship, distinguishing it from cases of total incapacity. This highlights the Shia juristic preference for fasting as the primary expiation when the pilgrim has the physical ability to endure it.
